questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A student simplified 120 − 40 ÷ 5 × 2 + 6 by first working out 120 − 40 and then going strictly from left to right. By how much was his answer less than the correct value?

solution.concept: Division and multiplication come before subtraction, working left to right

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
[(0.1)² + (0.01)² + (0.009)²] ÷ [(0.01)² + (0.001)² + (0.0009)²] = ?

solution.concept: Each term of the numerator is 10 times the matching term of the denominator
solution.explanation: 0.1 = 10 × 0.01, 0.01 = 10 × 0.001 and 0.009 = 10 × 0.0009, so every square in the numerator is 10² = 100 times the matching square below. The quotient is 100.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 forgets that the terms are squared; 1,000 cubes the factor 10; 0.01 inverts the quotient.

solution.concept: Here xy = 1; find x + y and use x² + xy + y² = (x + y)² − xy
solution.why_others_wrong: 62 is x² + y² (leaving out xy); 64 is (x + y)²; 65 adds xy to (x + y)² instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the value of the endless product 2^(1/2) × 4^(1/4) × 8^(1/8) × 16^(1/16) × …

solution.concept: Write every factor as a power of 2: (2ⁿ)^(1/2ⁿ) = 2^(n/2ⁿ); then add the indices
solution.explanation: The product is 2 raised to S = 1/2 + 2/4 + 3/8 + 4/16 + …. Then S/2 = 1/4 + 2/8 + 3/16 + …, and S − S/2 = 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … = 1. So S = 2 and the product is 2² = 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 takes the sum of the indices as 1 (the series 1/2 + 1/4 + …); 2√2 takes it as 3/2; 8 takes it as 3.

solution.why_others_wrong: 2,870 adds only the squares; 3,542 includes one term too many (up to 21 × 22); 2,660 uses k(k − 1) in place of k(k + 1).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y that holds for all their roots.
I. x² − 3x − 70 = 0
II. y² + 17y + 70 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise; compare the smallest x with the largest y
solution.explanation: I: (x − 10)(x + 7) = 0, so x = 10 or −7. II: (y + 7)(y + 10) = 0, so y = −7 or −10. The smallest x (−7) equals the largest y (−7), and every other pair has x > y. So x ≥ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y fails for the pair x = y = −7; x < y holds for no pair.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The two quadratics below have large constant terms. Factorise them and pick the relation that is true for every pair of roots.
I. x² − 31x + 240 = 0
II. y² − 35y + 304 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise each equation and look for a common root
solution.explanation: I: (x − 15)(x − 16) = 0, so x = 15 or 16. II: (y − 16)(y − 19) = 0, so y = 16 or 19. The largest x (16) equals the smallest y (16), and every other pair has x < y. So x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for x = y = 16; x > y holds for no pair.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I has one positive and one negative root. Solve I and II and compare x with y.
I. 3x² + 10x − 8 = 0
II. 2y² − 13y + 20 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Split the middle terms: 10x = 12x − 2x and −13y = −8y − 5y
solution.explanation: I: 3x² + 12x − 2x − 8 = (3x − 2)(x + 4) = 0, so x = 2/3 or −4. II: 2y² − 8y − 5y + 20 = (y − 4)(2y − 5) = 0, so y = 4 or 2.5. The largest x (0.67) is below the smallest y (2.5), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y reverse the comparison; every root of I is below every root of II.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The roots of both equations below are positive. Solve them and mark the relation between x and y.
I. 4x² − 21x + 27 = 0
II. 5y² − 13y + 6 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise by splitting the middle term
solution.explanation: I: 4x² − 12x − 9x + 27 = (4x − 9)(x − 3) = 0, so x = 3 or 2.25. II: 5y² − 10y − 3y + 6 = (5y − 3)(y − 2) = 0, so y = 2 or 0.6. The smallest x (2.25) exceeds the largest y (2), so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y fail for every pair; no root is shared, so the relation is strict.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Both equations have negative fractional roots. Solve them and choose the relation between x and y, if any, that holds for all their roots.
I. 6x² + 23x + 20 = 0
II. 3y² + 11y + 10 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise and place all four roots on the number line
solution.explanation: I: 6x² + 15x + 8x + 20 = (2x + 5)(3x + 4) = 0, so x = −2.5 or −1.33. II: 3y² + 6y + 5y + 10 = (y + 2)(3y + 5) = 0, so y = −2 or −1.67. x = −2.5 is below both values of y, but x = −1.33 is above both. No relation holds for every pair.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for x = −1.33; x ≥ y fails for x = −2.5; x > y and x ≤ y fail for the same pairs.
solution.final_answer: Option D: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y that holds for every pair of roots.
I. 8x² − 26x + 15 = 0
II. 2y² − 11y + 15 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise both; a common root makes the relation non-strict
solution.explanation: I: 8x² − 20x − 6x + 15 = (2x − 5)(4x − 3) = 0, so x = 2.5 or 0.75. II: 2y² − 5y − 6y + 15 = (2y − 5)(y − 3) = 0, so y = 2.5 or 3. The largest x (2.5) equals the smallest y (2.5), and every other pair has x < y. So x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for x = y = 2.5; x > y holds for no pair.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I is linear with decimal coefficients and equation II is quadratic. Solve both and choose the relation between x and y.
I. 0.6x − 1.5 = 0.35x + 0.5
II. y² − 22y + 117 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Collect the x-terms of I; factorise II
solution.explanation: I: 0.6x − 0.35x = 0.5 + 1.5, so 0.25x = 2 and x = 8. II: (y − 9)(y − 13) = 0, so y = 9 or 13. x = 8 is below both values of y, so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y would need x to be at least 9; solving I as 0.95x = 2 (adding the coefficients) is the usual slip.

II. y² + 5y + 4 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: x² − 4x = x(x − 4): x = 0 is also a root
solution.explanation: I: x(x − 4) = 0, so x = 0 or 4. II: (y + 1)(y + 4) = 0, so y = −1 or −4. The smallest x (0) exceeds the largest y (−1), so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y fail for every pair, even if x = 0 is (wrongly) dropped by dividing by x.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The roots of both equations are fractions. Solve them and choose the relation between x and y.
I. 9x² − 18x + 8 = 0
II. 10y² − 7y + 1 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Split the middle term: −18x = −12x − 6x and −7y = −5y − 2y
solution.explanation: I: 9x² − 12x − 6x + 8 = (3x − 4)(3x − 2) = 0, so x = 4/3 or 2/3. II: 10y² − 5y − 2y + 1 = (2y − 1)(5y − 1) = 0, so y = 1/2 or 1/5. The smallest x (0.67) exceeds the largest y (0.5), so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y fail for every pair; no root is shared, so the relation is strict.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The equations below have decimal coefficients. Solve them and choose the relation between x and y, if any.
I. x² − 1.3x + 0.4 = 0
II. y² − 1.1y + 0.28 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Find two numbers with the given sum and product (or multiply by 100 and factorise)
solution.explanation: I: the roots add to 1.3 and multiply to 0.4, so x = 0.8 or 0.5. II: the roots add to 1.1 and multiply to 0.28, so y = 0.7 or 0.4. x = 0.5 is less than y = 0.7 but more than y = 0.4. No relation holds for every pair.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y fails for 0.5 and 0.7; x ≤ y fails for 0.8 and 0.7; x < y and x ≥ y fail for the same pairs.
solution.final_answer: Option D: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I is given as a square. Take both square roots, solve II, and compare x with y.
I. (x − 2)² = 9
II. y² − 15y + 50 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: (x − 2)² = 9 means x − 2 = 3 or x − 2 = −3
solution.explanation: I: x − 2 = ±3, so x = 5 or −1. II: (y − 5)(y − 10) = 0, so y = 5 or 10. x = 5 equals one value of y and every other pair has x < y. So x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for x = y = 5; x ≥ y fails for x = −1.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I is exponential. Find every real x and y and choose the relation between them.
I. 2^(2x) − 6 × 2ˣ + 8 = 0
II. y² − 5y + 6 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Put t = 2ˣ: equation I becomes a quadratic in t, and t must be positive
solution.explanation: I: t² − 6t + 8 = 0, so t = 2 or 4, that is 2ˣ = 2 or 2ˣ = 4, giving x = 1 or 2. II: (y − 2)(y − 3) = 0, so y = 2 or 3. The largest x (2) equals the smallest y (2), and every other pair has x < y. So x ≤ y.
steps: max x = 2 = min y ⇒ x ≤ y
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for x = y = 2; x ≥ y would follow only if the roots t = 2, 4 were mistaken for the values of x.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the LCM of 2³ × 3² × 5 and 2² × 3³ × 7?

solution.concept: The LCM takes every prime to its highest power in either number
solution.why_others_wrong: 36 = 2² × 3² is the HCF; 2,72,160 is the product of the two numbers (360 × 756); 1,260 uses the lower power of 2 and 3² instead of 3³.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the unit digit of 13²⁰²⁵ − 7²⁰²⁵?

solution.concept: Unit digits of powers of 3 and 7 repeat every 4; 13²⁰²⁵ is the larger number, so borrow when needed
solution.explanation: 2025 = 4 × 506 + 1, so 13²⁰²⁵ ends in 3 and 7²⁰²⁵ ends in 7. 13²⁰²⁵ is larger, so the difference ends in 13 − 7 = 6 (borrowing 10).
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 uses the third place of the cycles (7 − 3); 0 uses the second place (9 − 9); 3 is the unit digit of 13²⁰²⁵ alone.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the smallest five-digit number that is exactly divisible by 7, 11 and 13?

solution.concept: A number divisible by 7, 11 and 13 is a multiple of their LCM, 7 × 11 × 13 = 1,001
solution.explanation: Multiples of 1,001: …, 9,009, 10,010, …. 9,009 has four digits, so the smallest five-digit multiple is 10 × 1,001 = 10,010.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10,001 = 73 × 137 is not a multiple of 1,001; 9,009 has only four digits; 10,101 = 1,001 × 10 + 91 is not a multiple of 1,001 (though it is divisible by 7 and 13).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many positive integers less than 1,000 leave a remainder of 1 when divided by 4 and a remainder of 2 when divided by 5?

solution.concept: Find the smallest such number; the rest follow at intervals of LCM(4, 5) = 20
solution.explanation: Numbers leaving 2 on division by 5: 2, 7, 12, 17, … The first that leaves 1 on division by 4 is 17. So the numbers are 17, 37, 57, …, 997. Count = (997 − 17) ÷ 20 + 1 = 50.
solution.why_others_wrong: 49 forgets to count the first term; 200 counts the numbers that satisfy only the remainder-2 condition; 100 divides 1,000 by 10 instead of 20.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A batter scores 84 runs off 60 balls. Her strike rate is the number of runs per 100 balls. What is her strike rate?

solution.concept: Strike rate = runs ÷ balls × 100
solution.why_others_wrong: 71.4 divides balls by runs; 124 adds 84 + 40 (the balls short of 100); 144 takes 84 ÷ 60 as 1.44.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Each month an employee puts 12% of her basic pay into her provident fund, and her employer adds an equal amount. In a year the total credited to her provident fund is ₹86,400. What is her monthly basic pay?

solution.concept: Each month 12% + 12% = 24% of the basic pay is credited
solution.explanation: Monthly credit = 86,400 ÷ 12 = ₹7,200. This is 24% of the basic pay, so basic = 7,200 ÷ 0.24 = ₹30,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹60,000 ignores the employer's equal share (12% only); ₹36,000 divides the yearly total by 2.4; ₹3,60,000 is the yearly basic pay, not the monthly.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sapling is 25 cm tall. Its height grows by 20% every month, each time on its height at the start of that month. How tall is it after 3 months?

solution.concept: Growth compounds: height = 25 × 1.2³
solution.why_others_wrong: 40 cm adds 20% of 25 three times (simple growth of 60%); 36 cm stops after 2 months; 51.84 cm runs for 4 months.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The price of cooking oil rises by 25%, and a family's spending on oil rises by only 5%. As a result the family now buys 4 litres less oil each month. How many litres did it buy each month before the price rise?

solution.concept: Quantity = spending ÷ price, so the new quantity is 1.05 ÷ 1.25 = 0.84 of the old
solution.explanation: New quantity = 1.05/1.25 = 84% of the old, a fall of 16%. 16% of the old quantity = 4 litres, so the old quantity = 4 ÷ 0.16 = 25 litres.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 litres takes the fall as 20% (25 − 5); 16 litres is the 16% itself; 21 litres is the new quantity.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two identical machines were bought at the same price. The first, bought 3 years ago, depreciates by 10% a year and is now worth ₹3,64,500. The second, bought 2 years ago, depreciates by 20% a year. What is the second machine worth now? (Each year's depreciation is on the value at the start of that year.)

solution.concept: Find the common purchase price from the first machine, then depreciate it for the second
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,91,600 applies 20% to ₹3,64,500 once; ₹3,00,000 uses simple depreciation (40% of ₹5,00,000); ₹2,33,280 depreciates ₹3,64,500 at 20% for 2 years.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A salesman can choose between two pay plans. Plan P: ₹6,000 a month plus 5% commission on the first ₹50,000 of sales and 4% on sales above that. Plan Q: ₹4,000 a month plus 6% commission on sales above ₹20,000. At what monthly sales do the two plans pay the same?

solution.concept: Write each plan's pay for sales S above ₹50,000 and equate
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,25,000 ignores Plan Q's ₹20,000 threshold (6,500 + 0.04S = 4,000 + 0.06S); ₹3,20,000 pays Plan P 5% on all sales; ₹1,60,000 pays Plan P 4% on all sales.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The sides of a triangle are in the ratio 3 : 4 : 5 and its perimeter is 84 cm. How long is the longest side?

solution.concept: The perimeter is the sum of the three sides: 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 parts
solution.explanation: One part = 84 ÷ 12 = 7 cm. The longest side = 5 × 7 = 35 cm.
solution.why_others_wrong: 28 cm and 21 cm are the other two sides; 42 cm takes half the perimeter.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If x : 15 :: 36 : 27, what is the value of x?

solution.concept: In a proportion, product of extremes = product of means: x × 27 = 15 × 36

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A's monthly salary is three-fifths of B's, and B earns ₹15,000 more than A. What is A's monthly salary?

solution.concept: The ₹15,000 gap is 2/5 of B's salary
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹37,500 is B's salary; ₹9,000 is 3/5 of ₹15,000; ₹25,000 takes the gap as 3/5 of B's salary.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The present ages of a teacher and a student are in the ratio 5 : 2. Three years ago the ratio was 3 : 1. How old was the teacher when the student was born?

solution.concept: Let the ages be 5k and 2k; the teacher's age at the student's birth is the age gap 3k
solution.explanation: (5k − 3) = 3(2k − 3) gives 5k − 3 = 6k − 9, so k = 6. Ages: teacher 30, student 12. The gap, 18 years, was the teacher's age when the student was born.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 and 12 are the present ages; 27 is the teacher's age three years ago.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If a : b = 3 : 5, what is (7a − 2b) : (3a + 4b)?

solution.concept: Put a = 3k and b = 5k; k cancels
solution.why_others_wrong: 29 : 27 swaps a and b (a = 5, b = 3); 29 : 11 inverts the answer; 21 : 29 drops the − 2b.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A piggy bank holds ₹1, ₹2 and ₹5 coins whose numbers are in the ratio 6 : 4 : 3. The ₹5 coins are worth ₹140 more than the ₹2 coins. What is the total value of the coins?

solution.concept: Take the numbers as 6k, 4k and 3k; their values are 6k, 8k and 15k rupees
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹460 leaves out the ₹1 coins; ₹290 and ₹1,160 use k = 10 and k = 40.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In an office the ratio of officers to clerks is 2 : 7. After 6 clerks are promoted to officers (no one joins or leaves), the ratio becomes 1 : 2. How many more clerks must now be promoted to make the numbers of officers and clerks equal?

solution.concept: Promotions move people between the groups; the total stays the same
solution.explanation: Let the numbers be 2k and 7k. (2k + 6) : (7k − 6) = 1 : 2 gives 4k + 12 = 7k − 6, so k = 6: 12 officers and 42 clerks, 54 in all. Now there are 18 officers and 36 clerks. Equal numbers means 27 each, so 9 more promotions.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 counts from the original 12 officers; 27 is the number in each group at the end; 6 repeats the first promotion.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Five years from now, Kabir will be three times as old as he was 15 years ago. How old is Kabir now?

solution.concept: Form one equation in Kabir's present age
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 is (5 + 15) alone; 30 is his age 5 years from now; 35 solves k + 5 = 3k − 45 as 2k = 70.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The present ages of P and Q are in the ratio 5 : 6, and Q is 4 years older than P. How old will P be 7 years from now?

solution.concept: The age gap of 4 years is 6 − 5 = 1 part
solution.explanation: 1 part = 4 years, so P = 5 × 4 = 20 and Q = 24. Seven years from now P will be 27.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 is P's present age; 31 is Q's age 7 years from now; 24 is Q's present age.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Twelve years ago, Sita was four times as old as her daughter. Six years from now, their ages will add up to 76 years. What is Sita's present age?

solution.concept: Six years from now both are 6 years older, so the present sum is 76 − 12 = 64
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 is the daughter's age; 50 is Sita's age six years from now; 32 is her age twelve years ago.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Six years from now the ages of X and Y will be in the ratio 7 : 5. X is 8 years older than Y. What is Y's present age?

solution.concept: The age gap does not change: 7 − 5 = 2 parts = 8 years
solution.explanation: 1 part = 4 years, so in six years X = 28 and Y = 20. Y's present age = 20 − 6 = 14.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 is Y's age six years from now; 22 is X's present age; 28 is X's age six years from now.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In 2026, a child's age (in completed years) equals the sum of the digits of the year in which the child was born. How old is the child in 2026?

solution.concept: If the child was born in 20ab, the age is 26 − 10a − b and the digit sum is 2 + a + b
solution.explanation: For a birth year 20ab: 26 − 10a − b = 2 + a + b, so 11a + 2b = 24. The only digits that work are a = 2, b = 1: born in 2021, age 5 = 2 + 0 + 2 + 1. (A birth year in the 1900s would need 11a + 2b = 116, which no digits satisfy.)
solution.why_others_wrong: A child aged 7, 6 or 4 would be born in 2019, 2020 or 2022, with digit sums 12, 4 and 6, which do not match.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of 12, 18, 25, x and 30 is 22. What is x?

solution.concept: Total = average × count
solution.explanation: Total = 22 × 5 = 110. The four known numbers add up to 85, so x = 110 − 85 = 25.
solution.why_others_wrong: 22 is the average itself; 30 takes the total as 115; 20 takes the known sum as 90.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average temperature from Monday to Thursday was 36°C and from Tuesday to Friday was 37°C. Friday's temperature was 9/8 of Monday's. What was Friday's temperature?

solution.concept: The two four-day totals differ only by Friday − Monday
solution.explanation: Friday − Monday = 4 × 37 − 4 × 36 = 4°C. With F = 9M/8, F − M = M/8 = 4, so M = 32°C and F = 36°C.
solution.why_others_wrong: 32°C is Monday's temperature; 40°C takes F − M as 8; 37°C is an average, not Friday's reading.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average age of the 40 employees of a branch is 32 years. The average age of the men is 36 and that of the women is 26. How many women work there?

solution.concept: Weighted average (alligation): men : women = (32 − 26) : (36 − 32)
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 is the number of men; 20 assumes equal groups; 12 uses the ratio 7 : 3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: When a 34-year-old member of a team retires and is replaced by a 22-year-old, the average age of the team falls by 1.5 years. How many members does the team have?

solution.concept: The total falls by 34 − 22 = 12 years, spread over all the members
solution.explanation: Fall in total = 12 years = team size × 1.5. Team size = 12 ÷ 1.5 = 8.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 is the fall in the total; 18 multiplies 12 by 1.5; 6 divides 12 by 2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of some numbers is 24. If the largest of them, 64, is removed, the average becomes 22. If instead only the smallest number is removed, the average becomes 25. What is the smallest number?

solution.concept: First find how many numbers there are from the first removal
solution.explanation: 24n − 64 = 22(n − 1) gives 2n = 42, so n = 21 and the total is 504. Removing the smallest: 504 − s = 25 × 20 = 500, so s = 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 takes 20 numbers in all (480 − 25 × 19); 24 is the average itself; 9 takes the total as 509.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average weight of A, B and C is 60 kg. When D joins them, the average becomes 62 kg. Then E, who is 3 kg heavier than D, replaces A, and the average weight of B, C, D and E becomes 61 kg. What is A's weight?

solution.concept: Work with totals: A + B + C, then D, then B + C
solution.why_others_wrong: 65 kg takes E as 3 kg lighter than D; 71 kg and 68 kg are E's and D's weights.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A bicycle bought for ₹3,600 is sold at a loss of 15%. What is the selling price?

solution.concept: Selling price = 85% of the cost price
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹4,140 adds 15%; ₹540 is the loss itself; ₹3,130 divides 3,600 by 1.15.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Selling an article at its marked price gives a profit of 32%. Selling it at a discount of ₹96 on the marked price gives a profit of 20%. What is the marked price?

solution.concept: The ₹96 discount equals the drop in profit, 32% − 20% = 12% of the cost price
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹800 is the cost price; ₹960 is the selling price after the discount; ₹1,200 takes ₹96 as 8% of the marked price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two shopkeepers buy the same item at the same cost. A marks it 20% above cost and allows a 10% discount; B marks it 30% above cost and allows a 15% discount. Which of them makes the larger profit, and by how much?

options.text: A, by 2.5% of the cost price
B, by 5% of the cost price
B, by 2.5% of the cost price

solution.concept: Selling price = cost × (1 + markup) × (1 − discount)
solution.explanation: A: 1.2 × 0.9 = 1.08, an 8% profit. B: 1.3 × 0.85 = 1.105, a 10.5% profit. B earns 2.5% of the cost price more.
solution.why_others_wrong: A earns less, not more; 5% subtracts the rates ((30 − 15) − (20 − 10)); the profits are 8% and 10.5%, not equal.
solution.final_answer: Option D: B, by 2.5% of the cost price

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A coat is sold for ₹2,520 after a discount of ₹480. What is the rate of discount?

solution.concept: Marked price = selling price + discount; the rate is discount ÷ marked price
solution.why_others_wrong: 19.05% divides the discount by the selling price; 20% takes the marked price as ₹2,400; 84% is the price paid as a share of the marked price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: After successive discounts of 20% and 15%, a fan costs ₹1,768. What is its marked price?

solution.concept: Price paid = MP × 0.80 × 0.85 = 0.68 × MP
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,720 adds the discounts to 35%; ₹2,210 undoes only the 20% discount; ₹2,386.80 adds 35% to 1,768.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A store gives 30% off its marked prices, and a further 10% off the reduced price for prepaid orders. On a prepaid order it makes a profit of 13.4%. What is its profit percentage on a cash-on-delivery order, which gets only the 30% discount?

solution.concept: Find the marked price as a multiple of cost from the prepaid order
solution.explanation: Prepaid: MP × 0.7 × 0.9 = 0.63 MP = 1.134 × cost, so MP = 1.8 × cost. Cash on delivery: 0.7 × 1.8 = 1.26 × cost, a profit of 26%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 23.4% adds 10 points to 13.4%; 13.4% is the prepaid profit; 80% is the markup on cost.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A television is marked ₹10,000. Shop X offers successive discounts of 15% and 10%. Shop Y offers a flat 20% discount followed by ₹500 cashback on the amount paid. Which shop is cheaper for the buyer, and by how much?

solution.concept: Work out the net amount at each shop
solution.why_others_wrong: Shop X, by ₹350 ignores Y's cashback (8,000 − 7,650); Shop X, by ₹150 reverses the comparison; 'both the same' adds X's discounts to 25%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the simple interest on ₹15,000 at 7% per annum for 146 days? (Take a year as 365 days.)

solution.concept: Time in years = 146 ÷ 365 = 0.4
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,050 is the interest for a full year; ₹210 uses 73 days; ₹840 takes 146 days as 0.8 of a year.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The simple interest on a sum for 3 years at 8% per annum is ₹480 more than the simple interest on the same sum for 2 years at 9% per annum. What is the sum?

solution.concept: Compare total rates: 3 × 8% = 24% and 2 × 9% = 18%
solution.explanation: The difference is 24% − 18% = 6% of the sum = ₹480, so the sum = 480 ÷ 0.06 = ₹8,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹48,000 uses the 1% gap between the rates; ₹6,000 divides 480 by 8%; ₹2,000 divides 480 by 24%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: ₹20,000 is deposited at simple interest. The rate is 7% per annum for the first 9 months and 8% per annum for the next 15 months. What is the total interest?

solution.concept: Convert months to years and add the interest of each period
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,950 swaps the two periods; ₹3,000 uses 7.5% for 2 years; ₹3,200 uses 8% for the whole 2 years.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sum is lent at simple interest. The interest for the 4th year alone is ₹720, and the amount after 6 years is ₹13,320. What is the rate of interest per annum?

solution.concept: Under simple interest every year's interest is the same
solution.explanation: Interest for 6 years = 6 × 720 = ₹4,320, so the principal = 13,320 − 4,320 = ₹9,000. Rate = 720 ÷ 9,000 = 8%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.4% divides 720 by the amount ₹13,320; 7.2% takes the principal as ₹10,000; 32% is the interest for 4 years as a percentage.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sum amounts to ₹13,310 in 3 years at 10% per annum compound interest, compounded annually. What is the sum?

solution.concept: Principal = amount ÷ (1.1)³
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹3,310 is the interest; ₹11,979 takes 10% off 13,310; ₹12,100 divides by 1.1 only once.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Meena borrows ₹50,000 at 12% per annum compound interest, compounded half-yearly. She repays ₹26,500 at the end of 6 months. How much must she pay at the end of the year to clear the loan?

solution.concept: Interest is 6% per half-year; reduce the balance by the repayment before the second half-year's interest
solution.explanation: After 6 months: 50,000 × 1.06 = ₹53,000; after repaying ₹26,500 she owes ₹26,500. After another 6 months: 26,500 × 1.06 = ₹28,090.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹29,680 charges interest on the full loan for the year and subtracts the repayment at the end; ₹26,500 leaves out the second half-year's interest; ₹29,500 compounds annually at 12%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The compound interest on ₹10,000 for 2 years, compounded annually, is ₹2,544. What is the simple interest on the same sum for 2 years at the same rate?

solution.concept: Find the rate from the amount: (1 + r)² = 12,544/10,000
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,272 halves the CI; ₹2,544 is the CI itself; ₹2,688 adds P × r² (₹144) instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sum amounts to ₹28,090 in 2 years at 6% per annum compound interest, compounded annually. How much interest is earned in the second year alone?

solution.concept: Second-year interest = 6% of the amount at the end of the first year
solution.explanation: Principal = 28,090 ÷ 1.06² = ₹25,000. After year 1: ₹26,500. Second-year interest = 6% of 26,500 = ₹1,590.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,500 is the first year's interest; ₹3,090 is the interest for both years; ₹1,685.40 takes 6% of the final amount.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: On a certain sum at a certain rate, the difference between the compound interest (compounded annually) and the simple interest is ₹160 for 2 years and ₹496 for 3 years. What is the sum?

solution.concept: For 2 years the difference is Pr²; for 3 years it is Pr²(3 + r)
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹4,000 takes the rate as 20%; ₹64,000 takes it as 5%; ₹1,600 divides 160 by 0.1 instead of 0.1².

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: On ₹1,60,000 at 20% per annum for 1 year, how much more interest is earned when the interest is compounded quarterly rather than half-yearly?

solution.concept: Quarterly: 5% for 4 quarters; half-yearly: 10% for 2 half-years
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,481 compares quarterly with simple interest (₹32,000); ₹1,600 compares half-yearly with simple interest; ₹34,481 is the quarterly interest itself.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A, B and C invest ₹1.2 lakh, ₹1.5 lakh and ₹0.9 lakh in a business for the same period. Out of a profit of ₹36,000, what is C's share?

solution.concept: Profit is shared in the ratio of capitals: 12 : 15 : 9 = 4 : 5 : 3
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹12,000 and ₹15,000 are A's and B's shares; ₹10,800 takes C's share as 30%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A starts a business with ₹72,000. Four months later B joins with ₹90,000, and B leaves 2 months before the end of the year. Out of a year's profit of ₹1,43,000, what is B's share?

solution.concept: B's money is in the business for 12 − 4 − 2 = 6 months
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹88,000 is A's share; ₹65,000 counts B for 8 months (ignoring that he left early); ₹71,500 splits equally.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A, B and C invest capitals in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3. A manages the business and first takes a fixed percentage of the profit as salary; the rest is shared in the ratio of capitals. What percentage must A's salary be so that A and C receive equal amounts in total?

solution.concept: Let A's salary be s of the profit; A gets s + (1 − s)/6 and C gets (1 − s)/2
solution.explanation: s + (1 − s)/6 = (1 − s)/2. Multiply by 6: 6s + 1 − s = 3 − 3s, so 8s = 2 and s = 1/4 = 25%. Check with a profit of 100: A = 25 + 12.5 = 37.5 and C = 37.5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 33⅓% gives A 44.4 and C 33.3; 20% gives A 33.3 and C 40; 50% gives A 58.3 and C 25 (per 100 of profit).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A grocer mixes 40 kg of rice costing ₹50 per kg with 60 kg of another variety. The mixture costs him ₹56 per kg. What is the cost per kg of the second variety?

solution.concept: Total cost of the mixture = cost of the first lot + cost of the second lot
solution.explanation: Mixture: 100 kg × 56 = ₹5,600. First lot: 40 × 50 = ₹2,000. Second lot: 5,600 − 2,000 = ₹3,600 for 60 kg, i.e. ₹60 per kg.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹65 swaps the two quantities (60 kg at ₹50); ₹62 treats ₹56 as the simple average of the two prices; ₹56 is the mixture's own price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A can holds 50 litres of pure milk. 5 litres are taken out and replaced with water, and then 5 litres of the mixture are taken out and replaced with water once more. How much water is now in the can?

solution.concept: After each replacement the milk is multiplied by (1 − 5/50) = 0.9
solution.explanation: Milk left = 50 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 40.5 litres, so water = 50 − 40.5 = 9.5 litres.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 litres forgets that the second 5 litres taken out already contained water; 40.5 litres is the milk; 5 litres counts only one replacement.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In what ratio must a 30% saline solution be mixed with a 75% saline solution to obtain a 48% saline solution?

solution.concept: Alligation: (weaker : stronger) = (stronger − mean) : (mean − weaker)
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 : 3 is inverted (it gives 57%); 1 : 1 gives 52.5%; 5 : 3 gives 46.875%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Three vessels of equal capacity are full of milk–water mixtures in the ratios 2 : 1, 3 : 2 and 4 : 3. Their contents are poured into one large drum. What is the ratio of milk to water in the drum?

solution.concept: Equal volumes: add the milk fractions of the three vessels
solution.explanation: Milk fractions: 2/3, 3/5, 4/7. Taking each vessel as 105 units: milk 70 + 63 + 60 = 193, water 35 + 42 + 45 = 122. Ratio = 193 : 122.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 : 2 adds the ratio terms (2 + 3 + 4 : 1 + 2 + 3), which treats the vessels as unequal; 122 : 193 is inverted; 193 : 315 is milk to the whole mixture.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A tank holds 30 litres of a 20% acid solution. How many litres of it must be drawn off and replaced with pure acid so that the solution becomes 40% acid?

solution.concept: Removing x litres removes 20% of x as acid; adding x litres of pure acid adds x
solution.explanation: Acid now = 6 litres. After the change: 6 − 0.2x + x = 40% of 30 = 12, so 0.8x = 6 and x = 7.5 litres.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 litres adds pure acid without drawing any off (6 + x = 0.4(30 + x)); 6 litres is the acid already present; 12 litres is the acid needed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A can holds 50 litres of pure milk. x litres are taken out and replaced with water; then 2x litres of the mixture are taken out and replaced with water. The can now holds 36 litres of milk. What is x?

solution.concept: Milk after two replacements = 50(1 − x/50)(1 − 2x/50); reject a root that does not fit the can
solution.why_others_wrong: 4⅔ litres treats the milk removed as simply x + 2x = 14 litres; 10 litres is the second draw (2x); 70 litres is the other root of the quadratic, impossible in a 50-litre can.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: P works twice as fast as Q, and Q works twice as fast as R. R alone can finish a job in 28 days. In how many days can P, Q and R together finish it?

solution.concept: Efficiencies 4 : 2 : 1; add the daily rates
solution.explanation: R does 1/28 a day, Q 2/28 and P 4/28. Together: 7/28 = 1/4 a day, so 4 days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7 days is P's time alone; 14 days is Q's time alone; 9⅓ days (28 ÷ 3) treats the three as equally fast.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A can finish a job alone in 20 days. After working for 5 days, he becomes 25% more efficient. In how many more days does he finish the job?

solution.concept: Work left after 5 days, divided by the new daily rate (1.25 × 1/20)
solution.explanation: In 5 days A does 5/20 = 1/4. New rate = 1.25/20 = 1/16 a day. Remaining 3/4 takes (3/4) × 16 = 12 days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 days ignores the improvement; 11¼ days cuts the time by 25% instead of dividing by 1.25; 17 days is the whole time, 5 + 12.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A man, a woman and a child do work in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1 per day. A team of 4 men, 4 women and 8 children can finish a job in 12 days. After 3 days, 2 men and 4 children leave. In how many days in all is the job finished?

solution.concept: Count the job in child-days; then divide the remainder by the new team's daily output
solution.explanation: Daily output = 4 × 3 + 4 × 2 + 8 × 1 = 28 units, so the job = 28 × 12 = 336 units. After 3 days, 84 are done and 252 remain. The new team (2 men, 4 women, 4 children) does 6 + 8 + 4 = 18 units a day, needing 252 ÷ 18 = 14 days. Total = 3 + 14 = 17 days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 14 days counts only the time after the change; 17.4 days treats everyone as equally efficient (16 people, then 10); 15 days assumes the job would only be delayed by the 3 days already worked.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A, B and C can finish a job alone in 10, 15 and 30 days respectively. They work in pairs in turn: A and B on day 1, B and C on day 2, C and A on day 3, A and B again on day 4, and so on. How long does the job take?

solution.concept: Take the job as 30 units (A 3, B 2, C 1 a day); find a three-day cycle and finish the remainder
solution.explanation: Day outputs: A + B = 5, B + C = 3, C + A = 4, so a 3-day cycle does 12 units. Two cycles (6 days) do 24, leaving 6. Day 7 (A + B) does 5, leaving 1. Day 8 (B + C, 3 a day) needs 1/3 of a day. Total = 7⅓ days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 days counts the last day in full; 7½ days divides 30 by the average 4 units a day, ignoring the order of the pairs; 5 days has all three working every day.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two pipes can fill a tank in 18 minutes and 27 minutes respectively. If both are opened together on the empty tank, how long will they take to fill five-sixths of it?

solution.concept: Combined rate = 1/18 + 1/27 = 5/54 of the tank per minute
solution.explanation: Combined rate = (3 + 2)/54 = 5/54 per minute. Time for 5/6 = (5/6) ÷ (5/54) = 9 minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 min 48 s is the time for the full tank; 18¾ minutes takes 5/6 of the average of 18 and 27; 13½ minutes halves the slower pipe's time.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A tap fills a 240-litre tank in 40 minutes. A leak in the tank lets out 1.5 litres a minute. How long does the tap take to fill the tank while the leak is working?

solution.concept: Tap rate = 240 ÷ 40 = 6 L/min; net rate = 6 − 1.5
solution.explanation: Net filling rate = 6 − 1.5 = 4.5 litres a minute. Time = 240 ÷ 4.5 = 53⅓ minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40 minutes ignores the leak; 32 minutes adds the leak to the tap (7.5 L/min); 160 minutes is how long the leak alone would take to empty the full tank.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Pipe A fills a tank in 10 hours and pipe B empties the full tank in 15 hours. A is opened on the empty tank at 6:00 AM and B is opened at 9:00 AM. When will the tank be full?

solution.concept: Fill with A alone for 3 hours, then the rest at the net rate 1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30 per hour
solution.explanation: By 9:00 AM A fills 3/10. The remaining 7/10 at 1/30 per hour takes 21 hours: 9:00 AM + 21 h = 6:00 AM the next day.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12:00 noon the next day opens both pipes at 6:00 AM (30 hours); 3:00 PM the next day ignores A's 3-hour head start and adds 30 hours to 9:00 AM; 4:00 PM the same day ignores B altogether.
solution.final_answer: Option B: 6:00 AM the next day

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Pipe A fills a tank three times as fast as pipe B, and takes 32 minutes less than B to fill it. How long will the two pipes take to fill the tank together?

solution.concept: If A takes t minutes, B takes 3t, and 3t − t = 32
solution.explanation: 2t = 32, so A takes 16 minutes and B 48 minutes. Together: 1/16 + 1/48 = 4/48 = 1/12, i.e. 12 minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 16 minutes is A's time alone; 48 minutes is B's; 8 minutes divides the 32-minute difference by 4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Pipes A and B fill a cistern in 6 hours and 8 hours respectively, and pipe C empties it. All three are opened on the empty cistern at 7:00 AM. C is closed at 9:00 AM, and the cistern is full at 11:00 AM. How long would C alone take to empty the full cistern?

solution.concept: A and B run for 4 hours; whatever they deliver beyond one cistern was removed by C in its 2 hours
solution.explanation: A + B fill 1/6 + 1/8 = 7/24 per hour, so in 4 hours they deliver 28/24 = 7/6 of the cistern. C removed the extra 1/6 in 2 hours, i.e. 1/12 per hour, so C alone empties it in 12 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 hours assumes C stayed open all 4 hours; 6 hours takes C to remove 1/3 in its 2 hours; 8 hours is B's filling time.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The speeds of A and B are in the ratio 3 : 4. Over the same route, A takes 20 minutes longer than B. How long does A take?

solution.concept: Times are in the inverse ratio of speeds: A : B = 4 : 3
solution.explanation: Times are 4 : 3; the difference of 1 part = 20 minutes, so A takes 4 × 20 = 80 minutes (B takes 60).
solution.why_others_wrong: 60 minutes is B's time; 140 minutes adds the two times; 100 minutes takes 5 parts.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A runner completes the first 400 m lap of a track in 80 seconds and the second 400 m lap in 100 seconds. What is her average speed over the two laps, in km/h?

solution.concept: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time; 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h
solution.why_others_wrong: 16.2 km/h averages the two lap speeds (18 and 14.4 km/h); 4.44 is the speed in m/s; 14.4 km/h is the second lap's speed only.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: From a crossing, Asha cycles due north at 12 km/h and Babu cycles due east at 16 km/h, both starting at the same time. How far apart, in a straight line, are they after 1 hour 30 minutes?

solution.concept: The two paths are at right angles: use Pythagoras on the distances covered
solution.explanation: Asha covers 12 × 1.5 = 18 km and Babu 16 × 1.5 = 24 km. Distance apart = √(18² + 24²) = √900 = 30 km.
solution.why_others_wrong: 42 km adds the two distances as if they rode in opposite directions; 6 km subtracts them as if they rode the same way; 20 km is the gap after only 1 hour.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: P and Q start at the same time from towns X and Y and travel towards each other. P is 25% faster than Q. They meet at a point 12 km from the midpoint of XY. What is the distance XY?

solution.concept: Distances covered are in the ratio of speeds, 5 : 4; P covers 12 km more than half and Q 12 km less
solution.explanation: P covers 5/9 and Q 4/9 of XY. The difference, 1/9 of XY, is 12 + 12 = 24 km, so XY = 9 × 24 = 216 km.
solution.why_others_wrong: 108 km takes the difference as 12 km instead of 24; 240 km treats the 24 km as 10% of the distance; 432 km doubles the answer.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A truck covers the first half of a route at 30 km/h. For the second half of the route, it runs at 40 km/h for half the time it spends on that half and at 60 km/h for the other half of that time. What is its average speed for the whole route?

solution.concept: Equal times: average = mean of the speeds; equal distances: average = harmonic mean
solution.explanation: On the second half the two speeds run for equal times, so that half's average is (40 + 60)/2 = 50 km/h. The two halves are equal distances, so the overall average = 2 × 30 × 50 ÷ (30 + 50) = 37.5 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40 km/h averages 30 and 50 arithmetically; 43.33 km/h averages 30, 40 and 60; 36.92 km/h treats the second half's speeds as covering equal distances (48 km/h).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat goes 18 km upstream in 1 hour 30 minutes. The stream flows at 3 km/h. How long will the boat take to come back the same 18 km downstream?

solution.concept: Upstream speed + stream = still-water speed; downstream = still-water speed + stream
solution.explanation: Upstream speed = 18 ÷ 1.5 = 12 km/h, so the boat's speed = 12 + 3 = 15 km/h and its downstream speed = 18 km/h. Time = 18 ÷ 18 = 1 hour.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 h 12 min uses the still-water speed 15 km/h; 45 minutes adds the stream twice (24 km/h); 1 h 30 min is the upstream time.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boatman rows 2 km against the current in 1 hour and 1 km along the current in 10 minutes. How long would he take to row 5 km in still water?

solution.concept: Still-water speed = (downstream speed + upstream speed) ÷ 2
solution.explanation: Upstream speed = 2 km/h; downstream speed = 1 km in 1/6 h = 6 km/h. Still-water speed = (6 + 2)/2 = 4 km/h. Time for 5 km = 5/4 h = 1 hour 15 minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 h 40 min uses 3 km/h (taking the downstream speed as 4 km/h, i.e. 1 km per 15 minutes); 50 minutes uses the downstream speed; 2 h 30 min uses the upstream speed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat's speed in still water is five times the speed of the stream. It goes 48 km downstream and comes back in 10 hours in all. If the boat's still-water speed is raised by 4 km/h (the stream unchanged), how long will the same round trip take?

solution.concept: First find the stream speed from the round trip, then recompute with the new boat speed
solution.explanation: Let the stream be s; boat = 5s, downstream 6s, upstream 4s. 48/(6s) + 48/(4s) = 8/s + 12/s = 20/s = 10, so s = 2 and the boat = 10 km/h. New boat speed = 14: 48/16 + 48/12 = 3 + 4 = 7 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 hours uses the new downstream speed both ways; 8 hours uses the new upstream speed both ways; 10 hours ignores the change.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A train running at 90 km/h crosses a 180 m long platform in 16 seconds. What is the length of the train?

solution.concept: Distance covered while crossing = train + platform
solution.explanation: 90 km/h = 25 m/s. In 16 s the train covers 400 m = train + 180, so the train is 220 m long.
solution.why_others_wrong: 400 m is the train and platform together; 580 m adds the platform instead of subtracting it; 1,260 m forgets to convert km/h to m/s (90 × 16 − 180).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A 125 m long train passes a man running at 6 km/h in the same direction in 10 seconds. What is the speed of the train?

solution.concept: Same direction: relative speed = train − man; the train covers its own length
solution.explanation: Relative speed = 125 ÷ 10 = 12.5 m/s = 45 km/h. Train speed = 45 + 6 = 51 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 45 km/h is the relative speed; 39 km/h subtracts the man's speed instead of adding it; 63 km/h adds 18 km/h (treating 6 km/h as 5 m/s).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A 280 m long train running at 50 km/h crosses a 220 m long train coming from the opposite direction on a parallel track in 15 seconds. What is the speed of the second train?

solution.concept: Opposite directions: relative speed = sum of the speeds; crossing distance = sum of the lengths
solution.explanation: Relative speed = (280 + 220) ÷ 15 = 100/3 m/s = 120 km/h. Second train = 120 − 50 = 70 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 120 km/h is the relative speed; 170 km/h treats the trains as moving the same way; 52.8 km/h uses only the second train's length (220 ÷ 15 m/s).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A train runs at 60 km/h. Its engine passes Arun, who is walking along the line in the same direction at 6 km/h, at 10:00 AM, and meets Bala, who is walking towards the train at 6 km/h, at 10:06 AM. At what time do Arun and Bala meet?

solution.concept: At 10:06 find the gap between the walkers; they then close it at 6 + 6 km/h
solution.explanation: In 6 minutes the engine goes 6 km past the point where it passed Arun, while Arun walks 0.6 km. So at 10:06 the gap between Arun and Bala is 6 − 0.6 = 5.4 km, closing at 12 km/h: 5.4 ÷ 12 = 0.45 h = 27 minutes. They meet at 10:33 AM.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10:36 AM forgets Arun's 0.6 km (6 ÷ 12 = 30 minutes after 10:06); 10:30 AM counts those 30 minutes from 10:00; 10:54 AM closes the gap at only Bala's 6 km/h, from 10:00.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two trains, 160 m and 140 m long, run towards each other on parallel tracks at 52 km/h and 56 km/h. From the moment their engines are 1.2 km apart, how long will it be until the trains have completely passed each other?

solution.concept: The engines must first meet (1,200 m) and then the trains must clear each other (160 + 140 m), at the relative speed
solution.explanation: Relative speed = 108 km/h = 30 m/s. Distance = 1,200 + 160 + 140 = 1,500 m. Time = 1,500 ÷ 30 = 50 seconds.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40 seconds stops when the engines meet; 10 seconds counts only the crossing itself; 45 seconds adds only one train's length.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The sides of a triangle are 9 cm, 12 cm and 15 cm. What is its area?

solution.concept: 9² + 12² = 15², so the triangle is right-angled with legs 9 and 12
solution.explanation: 81 + 144 = 225 = 15², so the angle between the 9 cm and 12 cm sides is 90°. Area = ½ × 9 × 12 = 54 cm².
solution.why_others_wrong: 108 cm² forgets the ½; 67.5 cm² and 90 cm² take the hypotenuse 15 cm as one of the perpendicular sides.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A hemispherical bowl of internal radius 9 cm is full of soup. The soup is poured into cylindrical cups, each of internal radius 3 cm and height 2 cm. How many cups can be filled?

solution.concept: Number of cups = volume of the hemisphere ÷ volume of one cup (π cancels)
solution.explanation: Hemisphere = (2/3)π × 9³ = 486π cm³. One cup = π × 3² × 2 = 18π cm³. Cups = 486 ÷ 18 = 27.
solution.why_others_wrong: 54 uses a full sphere; 81 forgets the cup's height (729 ÷ 9); 18 is the volume of one cup in units of π, not the number of cups.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A room is 10 m long, 8 m wide and 4 m high. It has one door 2 m × 1 m and two windows, each 1.5 m × 1 m. What will it cost to whitewash the four walls and the ceiling at ₹25 per m²?

solution.concept: Four walls = 2h(l + b); add the ceiling l × b; subtract the door and windows
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹5,600 forgets to subtract the door and windows; ₹3,600 whitewashes only the walls, without deductions; ₹7,475 also whitewashes the floor.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A square is drawn inside a circle of radius 10 cm so that all four of its corners lie on the circle. What is the area of the square?

solution.concept: The diagonal of the square is a diameter; area of a square = diagonal² ÷ 2
solution.why_others_wrong: 400 cm² takes the side equal to the diameter (the square around the circle); 100 cm² takes the side equal to the radius; 314 cm² is the area of the circle.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A solid metal cone with base radius 6 cm and height 24 cm is melted and recast into a solid sphere. What is the radius of the sphere?

solution.concept: Volume is unchanged: (1/3)πr²h = (4/3)πR³
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 cm takes half the cone's height; 3 cm takes half its radius; 9 cm drops both the 1/3 and the 4/3 and estimates the cube root of 36 × 24 = 864 (about 9.5).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Three faces of a cuboid that meet at a corner have areas 48 cm², 60 cm² and 80 cm². What is the volume of the cuboid?

solution.concept: (lb)(bh)(hl) = (lbh)², so volume = √(product of the three face areas)
solution.explanation: 48 × 60 × 80 = 2,30,400 = 480², so the volume = 480 cm³ (the edges are 8, 6 and 10 cm).
solution.why_others_wrong: 188 cm³ adds the areas; 960 cm³ doubles the volume (as in a surface-area formula); 2,30,400 cm³ forgets the square root.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A metal pipe is 1.4 m long. Its external diameter is 10 cm and its internal diameter is 8 cm. If 1 cm³ of the metal weighs 8 g, what does the pipe weigh? (Use π = 22/7.)

solution.concept: Volume of metal = π(R² − r²) × length
solution.why_others_wrong: 126.72 kg uses the diameters as radii; 88 kg treats the pipe as a solid rod; 3.96 kg forgets the 8 g per cm³.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Four equal circles, each of radius 7 cm, are placed so that each touches two others and their centres form a square. What is the area of the region enclosed between the four circles? (Use π = 22/7.)

solution.concept: Square of centres (side 14 cm) minus four quarter-circles (one full circle)
solution.explanation: The centres form a square of side 2 × 7 = 14 cm, area 196 cm². Inside it lie four quarter-circles, together one circle of area 22/7 × 49 = 154 cm². The enclosed region = 196 − 154 = 42 cm².
solution.why_others_wrong: 154 cm² is the area of one circle; 196 cm² is the whole square; 21 cm² halves the answer.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the total is 7 or 11?

solution.concept: Count the outcomes for each total and add (the events cannot happen together)
solution.explanation: Total 7: 6 outcomes; total 11: (5, 6) and (6, 5), 2 outcomes. P = 8/36 = 2/9.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/6 counts only a total of 7; 1/18 counts only 11; 7/36 counts (5, 6) and (6, 5) as one outcome.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: One card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 cards. What is the probability that it is a diamond or a black king?

solution.concept: The two events cannot overlap (no diamond is black), so add
solution.explanation: 13 diamonds + 2 black kings = 15 favourable cards. P = 15/52.
solution.why_others_wrong: 17/52 adds all four kings; 1/4 counts only the diamonds; 7/26 (14/52) counts only one black king.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A bag contains 3 red, 5 green and 2 yellow balls. A ball is drawn, its colour noted and it is put back; then a second ball is drawn. What is the probability that the two balls are of different colours?

solution.concept: P(different) = 1 − P(same colour); with replacement the draws are independent
solution.why_others_wrong: 19/50 is the probability of the same colour; 31/45 is the answer without replacement; 3/5 is a guess based on the three colours alone.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Three fair dice are rolled together. What is the probability that the total is at most 5?

solution.concept: Count the outcomes with totals 3, 4 and 5
solution.explanation: Total 3: (1, 1, 1), 1 way. Total 4: one die shows 2, 3 ways. Total 5: (1, 1, 3) in 3 ways and (1, 2, 2) in 3 ways, 6 ways. Favourable = 10 of 216, P = 10/216 = 5/108.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/54 leaves out the total of 5 (4/216); 1/36 counts only the total of 5 (6/216); 5/54 doubles the favourable count.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Three cards are drawn together at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 cards. What is the probability that exactly one of them is an ace?

solution.concept: Choose 1 of the 4 aces and 2 of the 48 non-aces, over C(52, 3)
solution.why_others_wrong: 1201/5525 is the probability of at least one ace; 432/2197 treats the draws as made with replacement; 3/13 multiplies 1/13 by the three cards.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many ways can 7 people stand in a queue if two particular people, Anil and Bina, must be at the two ends?

solution.concept: Fix the ends (2 ways), then arrange the other 5 in the middle
solution.explanation: Anil and Bina take the two ends in 2 ways; the other 5 people fill the middle in 5! = 120 ways. Total = 240.
solution.why_others_wrong: 120 forgets that Anil and Bina can swap ends; 5,040 is 7! with no condition; 1,440 arranges 6 people in the middle.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A group of 5 is to be chosen from 6 boys and 4 girls so that it has at least 2 girls and at most 3 boys. In how many ways can this be done?

solution.concept: Possible make-ups: 3 boys + 2 girls, 2 boys + 3 girls, 1 boy + 4 girls
solution.why_others_wrong: 120 counts only 3 boys and 2 girls; 246 removes only the all-boy groups from C(10, 5) = 252; 180 forgets the 1 boy + 4 girls groups.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many different 4-letter arrangements (not necessarily meaningful) can be made from the letters of the word COMMITTEE?

solution.concept: Letters: C, O, I once each; M, T, E twice each. Split by how many letters repeat
solution.explanation: All four different (from 6 distinct letters): 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 = 360. One pair + two different letters: 3 choices of pair × C(5, 2) = 10 others × 4!/2! = 12 ⇒ 360. Two pairs: C(3, 2) = 3 × 4!/(2! 2!) = 6 ⇒ 18. Total = 360 + 360 + 18 = 738.
solution.why_others_wrong: 360 counts only arrangements with four different letters; 3,024 treats all nine letters as different (⁹P₄); 48 counts selections of letters, not arrangements.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many self-help groups did the five branches finance in all?

solution.concept: Add the 'SHGs financed' column

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: A ball is drawn at random from a bag. What is the probability that it is green?
I. The bag contains 4 red balls and 6 green balls, and nothing else.
II. The bag contains only red and green balls, and there are 1.5 times as many green balls as red balls.

options.text: Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Both statements I and II together are needed

solution.concept: A probability needs only the proportion of green balls
solution.explanation: I: P = 6/10 = 3/5. II: green : red = 3 : 2, so green is 3/5 of the bag, whatever its size. Each statement alone gives 3/5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I alone' assumes II is useless because it gives no counts, but a ratio is enough; 'II alone' overlooks I; 'both' is more than needed.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: How long does pipe B alone take to fill the tank?
I. Pipes A and B together fill the tank in 12 hours.
II. Pipe A is twice as efficient as pipe B.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are needed

solution.concept: Two unknown times need a combined rate and a ratio
solution.explanation: I alone: 1/a + 1/b = 1/12 has many solutions. II alone: only a ratio. Together: rates 2 : 1 make 3 parts = 1/12, so B's rate = 1/36 and B alone takes 36 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I alone' and 'II alone' each leave a free unknown; 'neither' misses that the two together fix B's time.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both statements I and II together are needed

questions.question_text:

II. B is 25% more efficient than C.

options.text: Both statements I and II together are needed
Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not

solution.concept: II relates B to C, who does not appear in I; nothing fixes B's rate
solution.explanation: I gives a + b = 1/10 with two unknowns. II relates B and C only. Together, B's rate is still unknown (B could take 15 days and A 30, or B 20 days and A 20), so A's time is not fixed.
steps: I: one equation in A and B
B's rate never fixed ⇒ not sufficient
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Both' assumes II pins down B's rate, but it only links B to the unknown C; 'I alone' and 'II alone' are weaker still.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Statements I and II together are not sufficient

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements. Decide which statements are sufficient to answer it.
Question: What is the total surface area of the cuboid?
I. Its length, breadth and height are in the ratio 4 : 3 : 2.
II. Its volume is 192 cm³.
III. Its length is 8 cm.

options.text: Only I and II together are sufficient
Any two of the three statements together are sufficient
Either I and II together or I and III together are sufficient
All three statements together are necessary

solution.concept: Total surface area needs all three edges
solution.explanation: I + II: 24k³ = 192, so k = 2 and the edges are 8, 6, 4: area = 2(48 + 24 + 32) = 208 cm². I + III: 4k = 8, k = 2, the same cuboid. II + III: breadth × height = 24, but 6 × 4 and 12 × 2 give different areas (208 and 272 cm²), so II + III fail.
steps: II + III: b × h = 24, not fixed
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Only I and II' overlooks that III can replace II; 'any two' wrongly accepts II + III; 'all three' is more than needed.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Either I and II together or I and III together are sufficient

Question: A vessel holds a mixture of milk and water. Some of the mixture is drawn off and replaced with pure milk. What is the ratio of milk to water after this?
I. The vessel held 40 litres of the mixture, of which 25% was water.
II. 8 litres of the mixture were drawn off and replaced with milk.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Both statements I and II together are needed
Statements I and II together are not sufficient

solution.concept: The final ratio depends on the starting quantity, its water share and the amount replaced
solution.explanation: I alone does not say how much was replaced; II alone does not give the vessel's size or make-up. Together: water = 10 L at first; drawing off 8 of 40 litres removes 1/5 of it, leaving 8 L water, and milk becomes 32 L. Ratio = 32 : 8 = 4 : 1.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I alone' and 'II alone' each miss a needed quantity; 'neither' overlooks that together they fix the ratio.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements. Decide which statements are sufficient to answer it.
Question: In how many days can one man alone finish the job?
I. 3 men and 4 women together finish the job in 10 days.
II. 2 men and 6 women together finish the job in 10 days.
III. 6 men and 8 women together finish the job in 5 days.

options.text: Either I and II together or II and III together are sufficient
Any two of the three statements together are sufficient
Only I and II together are sufficient
All three statements together are necessary

solution.concept: Each statement is one equation in a man's rate m and a woman's rate w; check whether a pair is independent
solution.explanation: I: 3m + 4w = 1/10. II: 2m + 6w = 1/10. III: 6m + 8w = 1/5, which is just I doubled. I + II: subtracting gives m = 2w, so 10w = 1/10, w = 1/100, m = 1/50 — a man takes 50 days. II + III: the same as II + I. I + III: one equation repeated, so not sufficient.
steps: II + III works; I + III does not
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Any two' wrongly accepts I + III, which are the same equation; 'only I and II' overlooks II + III; 'all three' is more than needed.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Either I and II together or II and III together are sufficient
